title: Authorize unattended workflow runs with enforced capability envelopes
description:
## Problem Statement

LouiseLM can currently ask a human about ACP permission requests or auto-approve exact path and command scopes, but conversational intent, workflow authorization, harness permissions, and actual enforcement are disconnected. Tool identity is a poor proxy for consequence: a harmless tracker write may prompt while a destructive host operation may bypass LouiseLM entirely. Unattended workflow runs therefore need explicit, bounded authority whose enforcement and provenance can be demonstrated.

## Solution

Introduce run-scoped capability envelopes for policy-controlled workflow execution. The outer harness remains the hard ceiling; an operator approves the smallest proposed run envelope through a capability-diff review; every stage and worker receives only an intersected subset. LouiseLM's trusted policy layer classifies typed effects using concrete scopes and verified isolation, then allows, denies, escalates, delegates, or revokes them through trusted enforcement boundaries.

Reversibility is central but not sufficient. The model distinguishes reversible local mutation, destructive mutation, process execution, network access, data disclosure, credential use, external mutation, and cost. A sandbox changes blast radius but grants no authority: ordinary scoped repository work may use an isolated worktree, while untrusted code, unknown dependency installation, or broad unattended shell access requires launcher-attested confinement. Docker Sandboxes are one possible provider, not a product dependency or the policy source.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want to approve one inspectable, expiring envelope for an unattended run, so that harmless in-scope actions proceed without repeated prompts.
2. As an operator, I want high-consequence capabilities called out separately, so that “go ahead” never silently grants credentials, network access, cost, or external mutations.
3. As a workflow author, I want stages to propose narrower authority profiles without being able to authorize themselves.
4. As a coordinator, I want worker authority to attenuate through delegation, so that a child can never amplify the run's permissions.
5. As an operator, I want durable explanations for every policy decision and immediate revocation without storing secrets or pretending external effects were rolled back.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A workflow may propose an envelope, but unattended execution starts only after explicit operator approval. The effective envelope is the intersection of outer harness ceiling, approved run envelope, current stage, exact task/worker scope, and verified isolation capabilities.
2. The run-start UI presents a human-readable capability diff plus the machine manifest. It groups local roots, process execution and isolation, network destinations, credentials, external mutations, cost ceilings, delegation depth, expiry, and human gates. Routine scoped local effects may be approved together; credentials, external mutations, costs, open network, and weakened isolation require separate opt-ins. Harness-impossible capabilities are shown unavailable.
3. Grants expire with the workflow run. Project configuration, beads fields/labels, conversational phrases, named profiles, and remembered permissions may propose or narrow policy but cannot authorize a future run or expand its envelope.
4. Stages receive declared subsets. A worker receives the explicit intersection of run, stage, parent, task, and isolation capabilities. Credentials are separate and task-required; further delegation requires an explicitly delegable capability. Worker death/completion revokes its grant.
5. LouiseLM's trusted policy layer classifies typed effects for filesystem reads/writes, destructive mutation, process execution, network, disclosure, credentials, external mutation, and cost. It combines descriptors with actual arguments, normalized scopes/destinations, and launcher-attested isolation. Agent intent and friendly tool labels cannot lower risk; missing or contradictory evidence fails closed.
6. Arbitrary commands retain unknown secondary effects unless confinement makes those effects structurally impossible. Ordinary scoped edits/tests may run in isolated worktrees; untrusted code, unknown dependency installation, or broad unattended shell access requires verified confinement. No provider-specific sandbox dependency is required.
7. Every granted effect maps to a trusted enforcement boundary: a mediating launcher/harness, LouiseLM-owned executor, or verified filesystem/network/credential confinement. Startup computes coverage; uncovered effects are removed or force interactive mode. ACP permission prompts, prompts/tool descriptions, and agent promises alone never count as enforcement.
8. An optional out-of-envelope action is denied so the agent may adapt. A required action pauses at a durable checkpoint and emits one deduplicated escalation containing the requested effect and reason, rejecting boundary, affected scopes/destinations/credential class/cost, isolation evidence, and narrowest proposed expansion. Approval adds only that capability; rejection triggers replanning or graph blocking.
9. Policy prevents equivalent operations from evading a decision through splitting or disguise. Unknown/unclassifiable actions fail closed.
10. Revocation atomically narrows authority before cleanup, cancels affected requests where possible, revokes network/credentials at their enforcement boundaries, and stops children that cannot continue. Local work is preserved for inspection rather than auto-reverted. Completed external effects are explicitly remediated and never described as rolled back. Resumption requires a fresh grant.
11. A durable run manifest records approval/time, envelopes, policy/classifier version, session/worker/bead identities, isolation profile, scopes/destinations/credential classes/cost ceilings/expiry/delegation rules, and the enforcing boundary for each capability. An append-only decision log records allow, deny, escalate, narrow, expand, delegate, and revoke outcomes with matching policy rules.
12. Authorization records contain normalized effect classes and scopes, not prompts, full commands/diffs, environments, credential values, or tool payloads. Beads receives a concise summary and local evidence reference. Local records have explicit retention/deletion rules; required audit-storage failure pauses unattended execution.
13. Existing `ask-human`, `auto-approve-scoped`, and remembered permission behavior remains safe for interactive sessions. A remembered allow cannot exceed the active envelope; a remembered deny may narrow it. Unknown ACP requests remain non-automatic.
14. Deterministic tests cover envelope intersection, stage changes, separate high-consequence opt-ins, expiry, delegation attenuation, escalation deduplication, revocation ordering, privacy-bounded logging, sandbox-attestation mismatch, missing audit storage, and an adversarial mock agent attempting undeclared filesystem, process, network, and credential effects.

## Implementation Notes

- Extend the established permission-policy boundary rather than putting authorization logic in UI, prompts, tool names, or agent configuration.
- Keep policy classification pure and separate from Neovim UI, process launch, sandbox attestation, credential injection, and durable storage.
- Treat workflow definitions as proposals: `louiselm-qbr.3` owns persisted stages; this feature owns approval, enforcement, escalation, delegation, and revocation during execution.
- Reuse the quarantine and preserved-work handoff from `louiselm-qbr.6` when revocation or policy failure stops a worker.
- Docker Sandboxes evidence informed the generic isolation profile: direct read-write mounts, clone mode, host-side MCP execution, network policy, and credential proxies must be represented as capabilities/gaps rather than collapsed into a boolean “sandboxed”.

## Testing Notes

- Use pure policy tests plus the existing mock ACP agent; no real credentials, network, Docker, or coding-agent binaries.
- Model both cooperative agents that emit ACP permission requests and non-cooperative agents that omit or bypass them.
- Exercise fast-event/process boundaries through the production scheduling path when enforcement or revocation affects Neovim state.
- Verify logs by schema and absence of sensitive fields, not by snapshots containing real payloads.

## Out of Scope

- Treating reversibility as the only consequence dimension.
- Tool-name allowlists, prompt instructions, `ready-for-agent`, or conversational phrases as grants.
- A permanent project-wide grant or opaque “yolo” mode.
- Docker Sandboxes or any other isolation provider as a mandatory runtime dependency.
- Model/worker self-classification or self-attestation.
- Ambient inheritance of all parent permissions.
- Automatic rollback of completed external effects or concurrent local work.
- Raw transcript, environment, prompt, diff, command, credential, or tool-payload archives.

title: Run isolated parallel workers and coordinate integration
description:
## Problem Statement

LouiseLM's parallel milestone needs workers to execute independent beads concurrently without fragmenting tracker truth, colliding on claims, broadening their own authority, or closing work before integration is proven. Isolated Git worktrees make code work separable, but tracker state, lifecycle recovery, blocker promotion, and final integration still need one coherent ownership model.

## Solution

Run each worker as a first-class LouiseLM-spawned ACP session in an isolated Git worktree while every worker uses one canonical shared beads database. Workers may claim, comment, file findings, and hand off work in that graph; the coordinator alone selects authorized work, promotes discoveries to blockers, integrates branches, advances integration gates, closes tasks, and commits the canonical `.beads` export.

Candidate selection is a two-stage decision: `br` supplies the authorized currently-ready set, and `bvr` ranks or assigns parallel tracks only within that set. A worker receives one exact bead and atomically claims it with its attributable session identity.

The workflow policy makes handoff and rework first-class states. A worker moves `in_progress -> ready_for_integration` only with an atomic evidence comment. That state is not ready work and cannot be closed by a worker. After integration and combined verification, the coordinator satisfies an `integration_verified` gate and closes the bead. Rejected integration moves through `rework -> in_progress`; `rework` belongs to the policy's ready group.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want parallel workers isolated from one another while seeing the same task graph, so that concurrency does not fork tracker truth.
2. As a coordinator, I want graph eligibility separated from graph ranking, so that a high-scoring but unauthorized or out-of-scope bead is never dispatched.
3. As a worker, I want to record findings immediately and hand off verifiable work without pretending it is integrated.
4. As a coordinator, I want to validate discoveries before they become blockers and to resume preserved partial work after a blocker clears.
5. As an operator, I want dead-worker recovery and tracker checkpoints to preserve attribution and evidence without copying sensitive raw logs by default.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Each spawned worker is an attributable ACP session with its own worktree, cwd, branch/HEAD, permissions, transcript/session identity, and atomic beads claim.
2. Worker startup resolves `br where --json` to the canonical database, relying on upstream linked-worktree discovery (beads_rust commit 44c7a6f0 / PR #429, resolving through `commondir` to the primary checkout's `.beads`), present since `br` v0.4.0. A worker never runs `br init`, and a canonical-path mismatch fails startup before work begins.
3. The coordinator computes an authorized, currently-ready candidate set with `br`, intersects it with `bvr` ranking/parallel-track output, and dispatches an exact bead. `bvr` output alone cannot authorize or claim work, and its suggested bare status command is never used.
4. Workers may inspect and file discoveries freely, but execution scope expands only for a genuine blocker. A worker records a non-blocking discovery for later review and continues within its assigned scope.
5. A worker cannot promote its own discovery to a blocker. It files the issue with `discovered-from` provenance plus a structured blocker request and stops only when necessary; the coordinator validates the request before adding or changing a `blocks` edge.
6. On promotion, the coordinator adds the blocking edge first, returns the affected task to `open`, clears its claim with a durable reason, stops the worker, and quarantines its partial worktree/session. The dependency graph—not a separate `blocked` status—suppresses readiness. Closing the blocker makes the task ready again, preferentially resuming the preserved session/worktree when safe.
7. A strict `.beads/policy.yaml` defines `open -> in_progress -> ready_for_integration -> closed` and `ready_for_integration -> rework -> in_progress`. `ready_for_integration` is excluded from `workflow.status_groups.ready`; `rework` is included. The handoff transition requires an atomic evidence comment, and closure requires a coordinator-satisfied `integration_verified` gate.
8. Only the coordinator closes a work bead, and only after integrating its branch and running combined verification. Worker handoff evidence identifies the branch/HEAD, relevant tests/checks, known risks, and any preserved artifacts.
9. Positive lifecycle evidence of a known-dead spawned worker lets the coordinator recover it immediately: preserve/quarantine its worktree and session, record a durable recovery comment, release or reassign only that worker's claim, and retain attribution. Stale/abandoned thresholds remain the fallback for external sessions lacking lifecycle evidence.
10. Automatic recovery creates a bounded quarantine manifest by reference—session ID, claim, branch/HEAD, Git status, termination reason, timestamps, and relevant paths. Copying or exporting raw logs, prompts, tool payloads, environments, or a redacted evidence bundle requires a separate explicit action.
11. Only the primary/control checkout stages and commits canonical `.beads`. Workers write the shared database and allow atomic JSONL publication but never stage or commit `.beads`. After each successful integration the coordinator records the gate/closure, flushes beads, and commits integrated code with the complete point-in-time tracker snapshot. Shutdown or budget exhaustion performs a final tracker-only checkpoint if no later integration did.
12. Concurrent integration and tracker tests prove that worker claims remain attributable, JSONL publication is coherent under writes, no worker can close directly, rework resurfaces through `br ready`, blocker promotion suppresses then restores readiness, canonical database resolution fails closed, and recovery does not mutate unrelated claims or archive sensitive content.

## Implementation Notes

- Treat the coordinator as the authority boundary, not as the only tracker writer.
- Use beads workflow policy, strict transitions, transition comments, status groups, and gates rather than application-only labels for lifecycle semantics.
- `br` is upgraded to v0.4.0 (2026-08-23), which contains commit 44c7a6f0; the explicit `.beads/redirect` compatibility fallback has been retired rather than carried permanently. Linked-worktree resolution now relies solely on upstream discovery.
- Treat `bvr` as advisory graph analysis. It may return deferred or in-progress work and may emit unsafe claim commands, so intersect by bead identity with the `br`-authorized set.
- SQLite/database locking and atomic JSONL publication provide tracker concurrency. Git commits are durability checkpoints, not the source of per-mutation attribution.
- Keep open discovery cheap, but keep code execution inside the exact dispatched scope unless the coordinator authorizes a validated blocker.

## Testing Notes

- Use deterministic fake ACP workers and temporary linked worktrees; do not require live model credentials or network access.
- Exercise worker death before claim, after claim, after edits, during handoff, and after blocker discovery.
- Cover concurrent tracker writes and a coordinator checkpoint while workers continue writing; verify the commit is coherent and later mutations remain for the next checkpoint.
- Verify policy transitions and gates through `br`, including rejected direct closure and `rework` readiness.
- Verify the upstream automatic linked-worktree path (installed `br` v0.4.0, commit 44c7a6f0) resolves a fresh linked worktree's `.beads` to the primary checkout without spawning git.

## Out of Scope

- Per-worker beads databases or semantic JSONL reconciliation.
- Coordinator-only tracker writes or append-only worker journals.
- Opaque subagents as the primary execution worker.
- Workers selecting arbitrary high-ranked work, broadening scope, promoting blockers, integrating, or closing their own tasks.
- A separate `blocked` workflow status or labels standing in for lifecycle states.
- Automatic copying, exporting, or sharing of full session/log evidence.
- Redesigning `grill-me` challenger passes or the separate LouiseLM bug-report snapshot.

title: render-post fragments are not byte-identical across runs; CSS rule order varies
description:
`render-post.sh` documents its output as "a pure function of the current input"
and promises that "running twice against unchanged input is byte-identical".
It is not. Ten consecutive runs against identical input, in an identical
environment, produced four distinct fragment files. The difference is CSS rule
ordering, so the rendered page is unaffected — but the contract is false and
the test that claims to check it passes anyway.

## Observed

Found by QA case 9 of the round covering `ec19281..HEAD`, on build `daf3dfc`,
2026-08-20. Real post, real conversation excerpt (`:lines: 1481-1522`).

`blog.md` and `myst.yml` are byte-identical across runs. The fragment is not:

```
run  1  942aeb6aa0d2bbc13473e42d635ea066
run  2  b357a62c877f12da018565305d648c68
run  3  b357a62c877f12da018565305d648c68
run  4  07d64a69bd68ef675f020bcacd527080
run  5  5e4da75d9e1bbcd9942792ffa7a53d1e
...
```

Four distinct outputs across ten runs. Not environment-dependent — holding
`TERM` fixed still flips it:

```
TERM=dumb run 1  5e4da75d
TERM=dumb run 2  942aeb6a
TERM=dumb run 3  5e4da75d
```

The whole diff between two variants:

```
10d9
< .-conceal {}
12a12
> .-conceal {}
16a17
> .-markup-strong {color: #e78284; font-weight: bold}
18d18
< .-markup-strong {font-weight: bold; color: #e78284}
```

Rule order within the `<style>` block, and property order within a rule. The
`<pre>` markup is identical every time; the CSS is semantically identical every
time.

## Symptoms

- Re-rendering an unchanged post rewrites its fragment with different bytes.
- Fragments are written into the post directory and referenced from
  `myst.yml` `static_files`, so they are committed alongside a post — every
  re-render therefore dirties the working tree with a semantically null diff.
- No visual difference. The published page is correct in every variant.

## Root cause

Neovim's `:TOhtml` builds its `<style>` block by iterating the highlight groups
it collected with `pairs()`, whose order is unspecified in Lua and varies
between processes. `render-post.mjs` extracts that block verbatim
(`extractTagBlock`, then `buildFragmentDoc`), by design — `render-post.sh`'s
header states the style and `<pre>` are taken "unmodified (no selector
rewriting)".

So the non-determinism originates upstream in `tohtml.lua`, and this pipeline
faithfully preserves it. The real excerpt produces 11 rules
(`.-spell .-conceal .-nospell .-none .-markup-raw .rainbow2 .Whitespace
.Special .-tag-delimiter .-markup-strong .-tag`), which is enough for the
ordering to vary.

## Why it was not caught

`blog/scripts/test-render-post.sh` part 2 does exactly the right check —
`diff -rq "$run1_dir" "$run2_dir"` over fragments, `blog.md` and `myst.yml`.
It passes because its fixture is too small to expose the bug: the excerpts are
`:lines: 9-12` and `:lines: 16-20` of a hand-written fixture transcript that is
plain prose plus a two-line shell block and a three-line Lua snippet. That
yields a handful of highlight groups, and with few enough rules the iteration
order does not visibly change. The assertion is sound; the fixture is not
representative.

This is the same fixture-scale gap as louiselm-msg (skills discovery) and
louiselm-cmr (single-line tool titles): invented fixtures are well-behaved in
exactly the dimension the real data is not.

## Fix direction

There is a genuine conflict here, which is why this is filed rather than
patched.

Sorting the CSS is the obvious fix — normalise rule order and property order in
`render-post.mjs` before `buildFragmentDoc`. But `test-render-post.sh` part 1
asserts that the fragment's embedded `<style>`/`<pre>` match an *independent*
TOhtml capture byte-for-byte, and that capture would be unsorted. Sorting
therefore breaks part 1 unless part 1 normalises identically — at which point
"byte-for-byte against a real TOhtml capture", the property part 1 exists to
protect, is weakened to "byte-for-byte after our own normalisation".

Options, none free:

1. Sort in `render-post.mjs`, and normalise part 1's comparison the same way.
   Deterministic output; part 1 becomes a slightly weaker guarantee.
2. Sort in `tohtml-driver.lua` before the raw capture is written, so both the
   pipeline and part 1's independent capture see sorted input. Keeps part 1
   byte-exact against what the driver produces, but the driver is then no
   longer a transparent TOhtml wrapper.
3. Weaken the documented contract to semantic rather than byte equality, and
   compare parsed rule sets in part 2. Honest, but gives up the cheap
   `diff -rq` check and the "pure function of input" claim.
4. Fix upstream in Neovim's `tohtml.lua` and pin a version. Correct, slowest,
   outside this repo.

Recommend 1: it puts the normalisation where the pipeline already takes
responsibility for assembling the document, and the weakening of part 1 is
small and explicit. Whatever is chosen, `render-post.sh`'s header must stop
claiming byte-identical output until it is true.

## Acceptance

- Ten consecutive runs against unchanged input produce ten identical
  fragments.
- `test-render-post.sh` part 2's fixture is enlarged until it produces enough
  highlight groups to have caught this — otherwise the same gap remains.
- `render-post.sh`'s header contract matches the implemented behaviour.

## Not covered

- Whether `.rainbow2` and similar plugin-provided groups make the group set
  itself vary between runs (as opposed to only its order) is unverified; every
  observed variant had the same 11 rules, but that is 10 samples.
- Neovim's `tohtml.lua` has not been read to confirm `pairs()` specifically;
  the unspecified-order conclusion is inferred from the symptom.
close_reason:
Fixed by canonicalising the TOhtml <style> block inside buildFragmentDoc (blog/scripts/render-post.mjs): rules sorted by selector, declarations sorted within each rule, code-unit comparison so the output does not depend on locale. <pre> is still passed through verbatim.

Root cause verified at source rather than inferred: Neovim 0.12.2 tohtml.lua has TWO pairs() loops, line 1004 over highlight groups (rule order) and line 1032 over a group's attributes (declaration order). Sorting only rule order left 5 distinct blocks out of 10 runs; sorting both collapses to 1.

Boundary is better than the issue proposed. The issue expected part 1 of test-render-post.sh to need a matching normalisation and to be weakened by it. It does not: part 1 builds its expected fragment by calling buildFragmentDoc itself, so normalising inside that function keeps part 1 byte-exact against an independent real TOhtml capture with no change and no loss of guarantee. The filed conflict does not exist at that boundary.

All three acceptance criteria met:
- Ten consecutive runs against unchanged input are byte-identical (new part 2 check; two runs used to pass by luck).
- Part 2's fixture enlarged until it would have caught this: the excerpts now carry bold, italic, inline code, a link, a blockquote, a list and two fenced languages, producing 30 CSS rules against the old fixture's handful. Proof it is now representative: with the enlarged fixture and the fix reverted, the suite fails 4 checks (part 1, part 2 two-run, part 2 ten-run, part 2b) where it previously passed 20/20 -- the old fixture was masking this in three more places than the one it was filed against.
- render-post.sh's header contract and render-post.mjs's overview no longer claim the CSS is unmodified, and state what the canonicalisation is and why.

Independent verification outside the fixture: the 10 real TOhtml captures used to reproduce the bug (7 distinct raw style blocks) produce exactly 1 distinct fragment after buildFragmentDoc.

Gates: blog/scripts/test-render-post.sh 21 passed 0 failed; stylua --check . exit 0; lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning no problems found; MiniTest full suite Fails (0) Notes (0); git diff --check clean.

Not done, deliberately: option 4 from the issue, fixing pairs() ordering upstream in Neovim's tohtml.lua. It is still the root-cause fix, but it now has no user-visible effect on this pipeline.

comments.author: lotso
comments.text:
Both 'Not covered' items resolved during the fix.

1. The group SET is stable; only ordering varies. Ten captures of a rich markdown buffer (bold, italic, inline code, link, blockquote, list, bash fence, lua fence -> 30 rules) gave 7 distinct raw style blocks, but parsing them into {selector -> sorted declarations} maps yielded exactly 1 distinct map, and 1 distinct selector set. So .rainbow2 and friends do not come and go. Sorting is therefore sufficient, not just cosmetic.

2. pairs() confirmed at source, not inferred. Neovim 0.12.2, runtime/pack/dist/opt/nvim.tohtml/lua/tohtml.lua: line 1004 'for hlid, name in pairs(state.highlights_name)' emits one rule per highlight group (rule order), and line 1032 'for attr, val in pairs(c)' emits the declarations inside a rule (property order). Two independent pairs() loops, which is why normalising rule order alone was not enough -- sorting only the style lines still left 5 distinct blocks out of 10.

Fix took option 1 but at a better boundary than the issue proposed. The issue assumed normalising in render-post.mjs *before* buildFragmentDoc, which would have forced test-render-post.sh part 1 to normalise separately and weakened it. But part 1 builds its expected fragment BY CALLING buildFragmentDoc itself, so putting normalizeStyleBlock inside buildFragmentDoc makes part 1 normalise identically for free. Part 1 keeps its exact property: 'fragment == the same builder applied to an independent real TOhtml capture'. Nothing was weakened, and the conflict that got this filed rather than patched does not exist at that boundary.

The <pre> block was verified deterministic across all 10 captures and is still passed through verbatim.

title: Agent
description: A named, configured ACP entry that LouiseLM can start a session with.

title: Queued prompt can remain stuck after active turn becomes ready
description:
Observed during live LouiseLM chat QA on 2026-08-22: while the model was responding, pressing Enter queued a prompt. After the agent finished, the status remained Model responding instead of returning to Your turn / advancing the queued prompt.

Root cause: lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua releases queued prompts only from the turn_done handler. The session lifecycle publishes state_changed ready as the authoritative idle transition separately; if the terminal turn event is lost or delivered out of order, the queued prompt and its marker remain indefinitely. The UI currently has no ready-state fallback.

Acceptance:
- A queued prompt is released when its session emits state_changed with status ready, even if no turn_done event is delivered.
- The normal state_changed + turn_done sequence submits the queued prompt at most once.
- Existing queued prompt, error, cancellation, disposal, and status rendering behavior remains green.
close_reason: Fixed queued prompt release on ready state transition; focused and full suites pass.

comments.text: Implemented the narrow UI fix: a ready state_changed event now releases a queued prompt, while clear_queued_prompt keeps the subsequent turn_done from resubmitting it. Added regression coverage for ready without turn_done and normal state_changed + turn_done ordering. Focused chat suite: 78 passed; full mini.test suite: 324 passed; stylua --check and lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning passed. Test harness retains existing skill-discovery/write warnings without failures.

title: Private blog-publishing pipeline for louiselm session transcripts
description:
## Problem Statement

Turning an interesting agent conversation into a blog post currently requires manual, repetitive steps: copying chat buffer text by hand into a markdown file (lossy — collapses tool calls to one-line summaries, truncates commands and output), hand-building a MyST project from scratch, and no way to render a quoted excerpt with the same Neovim/Catppuccin/Tree-sitter styling the author actually saw, while keeping the rest of the post in a separate blog theme.

## Solution

A private, louiselm-adjacent publishing pipeline for turning louiselm session transcripts into blog posts. One real plugin command (LouiselmToMarkdown) exports a session's full structured transcript (not a lossy buffer scrape) to markdown. A blog/ directory at the repo root (sibling to android/ and capture-service/, not documented as a plugin feature) holds a multi-post MyST site plus two private scripts: one scaffolds a new post (optionally auto-exporting named sessions into it), the other batch-renders every excerpt a finished post quotes through the author's real Neovim config into scoped, dual-theme-safe HTML fragments, ready for a plain myst build with zero Neovim dependency in CI.

## User Stories

1. As the author, I want to export any louiselm session's full transcript to markdown from its structured JSONL data (not the truncated chat buffer), so quoting a conversation in a post does not require re-digging through raw logs.
2. As the author, I want to scaffold a new post directory in one command, so starting a post from "I want to blog about lines X-Y in session A and lines Z-W in session B" does not require manually creating folders.
3. As the author, I want that scaffold command to optionally take session ids and auto-export plus auto-stub a literalinclude block for each, so the moment scaffolding finishes, every source I named is already present and ready to quote from.
4. As the author, I want a single batch step that renders every nvim-transcript-tagged excerpt in a finished post through my real Neovim config (Catppuccin, Tree-sitter) into namespaced HTML+CSS, so the published transcript looks exactly like what I saw on screen, without polluting the blog's own theme.
5. As the author, I want the rendered output committed and CI to just run myst build with no Neovim dependency, so publishing does not require reproducing my personal editor setup inside a CI container.
6. As the author, I want the finished site published at blog.bartab.fr via GitLab Pages from this same repo, so there is no second repo to maintain for a workflow that is fundamentally "I am already in louiselm."

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a louiselm session id, running LouiselmToMarkdown produces a markdown file containing the full transcript reconstructed from the session's structured JSONL (full tool commands and results, not one-line summaries).
2. Given blog/scripts/create-blog.sh <name>, a blog/post-<name>/ directory is created containing an empty blog.md and an empty conversations/ folder.
3. Given blog/scripts/create-blog.sh <name> <session-id>..., the same scaffold is created, conversations/<session-id>.md exists for each session id (via the same export path as LouiselmToMarkdown), and blog.md contains one literalinclude block per session pointing at its exported file.
4. Given a blog.md with one or more code blocks tagged :class: nvim-transcript, running the batch render script produces fragment HTML for each block plus one shared, namespaced CSS file, using the author's real Neovim config — and running it again is idempotent (safe to re-run after editing line ranges).
5. Given the rendered fragments are committed, myst build --html succeeds using only MyST and Node — no Neovim process is spawned during the build.
6. The GitLab CI pipeline in this repo builds and deploys blog/ to blog.bartab.fr via GitLab Pages on push, without requiring Neovim in the CI image.

## Implementation Notes

- LouiselmToMarkdown follows the existing Louiselm* command registration pattern (alongside LouiselmResume, LouiselmSessionId, etc. in the chat command module) and reads from the same structured session/transcript data those commands already have access to, not the rendered chat buffer.
- blog/ is a new top-level directory, siblings android/ and capture-service/ — precedent already exists in this repo for non-Neovim-plugin material living alongside lua/.
- The scaffold and render scripts are plain shell/Node scripts under blog/scripts/, not Neovim commands — this tooling is intentionally not part of the plugin's discoverable command surface.
- The render script needs to invoke the author's real Neovim configuration headlessly (not nvim --clean) to get accurate Catppuccin/Tree-sitter output — reusing whatever TOhtml/tohtml.tohtml() wrapper already exists or building a minimal one.
- CSS namespacing (scoping generated Neovim highlight-group classes under a wrapper class) is required so the blog's own theme and the Neovim theme cannot collide on the same page.
- MyST config (blog/myst.yml, blog/blog.css) should be structured as a real multi-post project from the start, not a single-page site — a second post is expected.

## Testing Notes

- LouiselmToMarkdown output should be tested against a fixture session JSONL, asserting full tool commands/results appear (not truncated).
- The scaffold script's directory-creation and auto-stub behavior can be tested as a plain shell/script test (given a fake session export, assert the resulting blog.md contents).
- The render script's CSS-namespacing step is the highest-risk piece — worth a focused test asserting generated selectors are correctly prefixed and that two renders of the same input are byte-identical (supports the idempotency acceptance criterion).
- No UI/Neovim-buffer testing needed — this is headless tooling.

## Out of Scope

- Writing the first post's prose, choosing excerpt line ranges, and designing blog.css's actual visual theme — tracked separately, not part of this feature.
- Any interactive/visual-selection tool for previewing excerpts while authoring (considered and explicitly rejected — plain Neovim navigation is sufficient for picking line ranges).
- Any MyST build-time JS plugin that renders excerpts live during myst build/myst start — rendering is a separate, explicit, pre-build step by design, to avoid needing Neovim in CI.
- Deploying/configuring anything at the bartab.fr root domain — this feature only concerns the blog.bartab.fr subdomain.

title: Make skill discovery deterministic and symlink-aware
description:
## Goal

Discover local skills predictably across configured roots while preserving useful paths and diagnosing duplicates or unsafe-looking topology.

## Scope

- In scope: process global skill roots in configuration order; within each root sort deterministically by skill name and configured path.
- In scope: first valid duplicate skill name wins, later names are reported as shadowed, and the same canonical file is deduplicated.
- In scope: expand absolute paths and `~`; resolve relative roots against the session working directory. Health checks resolve them against Neovim's current working directory and say so.
- In scope: support symlinked roots and skill directories, detect canonical cycles/duplicates, preserve the configured-root alias in advertised absolute locations, and warn when a symlink resolves outside its root.
- In scope: continue past unreadable or invalid individual skills with one deduplicated user warning and full details available to diagnostics.
- In scope: refresh discovery whenever the picker opens and read the selected file at selection time.
- Out of scope: automatic project-local roots, a trust database, policy transport, and catalog budgeting.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Root order, not global absolute sorting, decides duplicate-name precedence.
2. Discovery order and diagnostics are stable across runs.
3. Canonical aliases do not create duplicate skills or traversal loops.
4. Catalog/picker locations preserve the user-configured alias rather than exposing a canonical dotfiles target.
5. Escapes outside a configured root remain usable but produce a source-to-target warning.
6. Relative-root behavior is covered for both sessions and checkhealth.
7. MiniTest covers duplicate names, identical canonical files, symlinked roots/directories, cycles, outside-root targets, unreadable files, and picker refresh behavior.

## Testing

Use temporary directory fixtures with real symlinks where supported. Keep path-policy tests separate from YAML semantic fixtures.

## Notes

Configured skill roots are trusted prompt/plugin-like input. Diagnostics inform the user; they do not create a new authorization system.
close_reason: Implemented deterministic root-order discovery, canonical symlink traversal and diagnostics, session-relative picker refresh, selection-time reads, and checkhealth coverage

title: Add README licence section framing the choice as serving reach
description:
Add a licence section to `README.md` that states the choice and the reasoning behind it.

## Content

- LouiseLM is MIT licensed.
- The licence is chosen to serve reach: the project's usefulness depends on being installable anywhere with no friction.
- If reach stops being the binding constraint, the choice will be revisited.
- Link to the trademark policy and the political statement.

## Why the last point matters

Publishing the expiry condition is what makes a future relicense a disclosed term rather than a rug-pull. It costs nothing now and is the difference between a relicense that is legitimate and one that is radioactive.

## Acceptance criteria

- README has a licence section containing all four points.
- Wording does not promise perpetuity, and does not read as a threat either.
- Links resolve.
close_reason: Published the complete README licensing posture with valid policy links.

title: Make the repo the substrate for cross-adapter agent context
description:
## Problem Statement

louiselm is an interface to ACP adapters, not a Claude-only tool. But the durable context an agent accumulates while working on this repo — conventions, design decisions, the maintainer's workflow — has been landing in Claude Code's private per-project memory store. Any other adapter reading this repo sees none of it.

The inverse failure exists too. `AGENTS.md` is the adapter-neutral instruction file, and it is not auto-loaded by Claude Code: there is no root `CLAUDE.md` and no setting pointing at it. So the repo currently has one context store that only Claude reads and one that Claude ignores, and neither is a shared substrate.

Concretely: `AGENTS.md` is 214 lines across 11 sections and does not mention beads once, even though beads is the task graph the whole project runs on. An agent entering this repo cold has no way to learn that findings should be filed as beads. Meanwhile five of seven notes in Claude's project memory are repo content that was misfiled there purely because it was the path of least resistance.

## Solution

Make the repository the substrate for durable agent context, and reduce per-adapter memory to only what is genuinely adapter-specific.

The routing rule, by two axes:

- **About louiselm, adapter-independent** → the repo.
- **About the maintainer, cross-project** → that adapter's own user-level instructions.
- **About one adapter's harness quirks** → that adapter's project memory. Applied honestly this is nearly empty, which is the correct outcome and not evidence the rule is wrong.

Within the repo, placement follows the anchor:

- Anchored to a specific work item → a `br` comment on that issue, so it travels with the issue and needs no separate discovery mechanism.
- A standing convention true for every session → `AGENTS.md`.
- The maintainer's own workflow loop → an explicitly non-binding example document.

`AGENTS.md` becomes the single entrypoint. Every adapter is pointed at it rather than given its own parallel instruction file, because parallel instruction files diverge silently and the divergence surfaces at the worst possible moment.

## User Stories

1. As an agent entering this repo through any ACP adapter, I want the work-tracking conventions stated in the file I already read on entry, so that I file findings as beads instead of inventing my own process.
2. As the maintainer, I want a decision recorded during a session to survive regardless of which adapter recorded it, so that switching adapters does not silently lose context.
3. As a contributor or agent, I want the maintainer's personal workflow clearly marked as an example rather than a requirement, so that I can invent my own loop without believing I am violating a contract.
4. As the maintainer, I want my own loop written down as prose now, so that the future workflow-config feature has a spec to implement against rather than being reconstructed from memory.
5. As an agent picking up a deferred issue months later, I want design context attached to that issue, so that I do not need the conversation that produced it.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a fresh clone opened by any adapter that reads `AGENTS.md`, when the agent reads it, then the beads work-tracking conventions are present and stated in the file's own imperative register.
2. Given Claude Code opening this repo, when it auto-loads project instructions, then it is directed to `AGENTS.md` and no instruction content exists outside it.
3. Given the example workflow document, when any reader reaches it, then it self-identifies as a non-binding example, and `AGENTS.md` says the same where it links out.
4. Given the deferred workflow-engine issues, when someone opens them, then the in-progress-first triage requirement is attached as a comment.
5. Given Claude's project memory folder, when it is inspected after migration, then it contains only genuinely Claude-specific harness notes, and every repo fact previously held there exists in the repo.
6. Given `AGENTS.md`, when the workflow section is read, then it references `br robot-docs` for command syntax rather than duplicating a command cheatsheet.

## Implementation Notes

- Affected: `AGENTS.md` (new section, renumbering), a new root `CLAUDE.md` pointer, a new example workflow document under `docs/`, `br` comments on the deferred workflow-engine issues, and Claude's project memory store.
- **Do not use `br agents --add`.** It emits roughly 60 lines of generic beads tutorial in a `<!-- br-agent-instructions-v1 -->` block. Three problems: the register clashes with `AGENTS.md`, which is terse and imperative; it teaches command syntax discoverable from `br --help` while saying nothing about this project's actual conventions; and hand-edits inside a versioned generated block are destroyed by `br agents --update`, so the conventions would live in the one place designed to be overwritten.
- The workflow section is inserted as section 2, immediately after Project Scope, not appended at the end. Reading order should be *what this project is* → *how work is found and tracked* → *how code must be written*, because an agent finds work before it writes any. Renumbering the existing sections is mechanical churn and acceptable; section 1 already states breaking changes are fine and there are no external users.
- The example document lives at a `docs/` path rather than root. A root-level uppercase filename reads as normative regardless of any disclaimer it carries, which is the precise misreading to avoid.
- The `CLAUDE.md` pointer must stay a pointer. Real content in it beside a real `AGENTS.md` guarantees drift.
- The example workflow document is the first draft of the workflow-config that louiselm intends to ship as an example. It should be written knowing that, without over-committing to a config schema that does not exist yet.

## Testing Notes

- No automated tests. Verification is documentary: read `AGENTS.md` top to bottom as if entering cold and confirm the work-tracking conventions are learnable; confirm the example document is unambiguously non-binding on first read.
- Confirm no instruction content is duplicated between `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`.
- Confirm nothing was lost in the memory migration by checking each migrated note has a repo destination.

## Out of Scope

- Cross-adapter portability of *session/conversation history*. That is a much larger problem already implied by the attention-control-plane roadmap, and is not solved as a side effect of relocating notes.
- Any wrapper script around `br`/`bv`, and any project-scoped skill override for them. Both were considered and rejected: they relocate a personal preference into the repo without it becoming a real louiselm capability.
- Building the workflow-config engine itself. This feature produces the prose spec, not the implementation.
- Resolving how completed QA review rounds get archived. Tracked separately; it wants full attention rather than being decided in passing.
- Rewriting the existing 11 sections of `AGENTS.md`. Purely additive apart from renumbering.
close_reason: All four children complete: AGENTS.md work-tracking section, CLAUDE.md pointer, docs/example-workflow.md, br comments on qbr.3/qbr.5, memory migration

title: Give qa-review rounds a mandatory archiving/closing step backed by beads
description:
## Problem Statement

A `qa-review` round produces a working file (`QA_REVIEW.md`-style) that
accumulates the plan, case-by-case results, and narration for the round. When
the round ends, nothing decides what happens to that file — commit it, fold
it into beads, or delete it. This has now happened twice in a row
(transcript-export/blog-publishing round, then the permissions round), each
time ending with the same unresolved question and an untracked markdown file
left sitting in the repo root. Findings filed during a round (via
`to-beads-bug`, which already works correctly) also end up orphaned from the
round that produced them — nothing records which round found which bug.

Resolved via grill-me session against `louiselm-iyy`, which had a concrete
proposal already on record from an earlier session; this feature adopts that
proposal.

## Solution

A `qa-review` round closes into exactly one bead, which becomes the round's
sole durable record:

1. **One bead per round.** Type `chore`, label `qa-round`, created with
   `--description-file <working-file>` so the round's plan/results become the
   bead description, and `--external-ref <session-id>` so the round is tied
   to the session that ran it.
2. **Findings hang off it as children.** Continues using the existing,
   already-working `to-beads-bug` chain: `br create -t bug --parent
   <round-id>`. This makes "which round found this?" answerable from the
   graph.
3. **Cases stay flat.** Individual test cases inside the round are never
   promoted to their own beads — they aren't independently actionable, have
   no lifecycle of their own, and beading them would add ceremony for no
   graph benefit. Only findings (bugs) get promoted.
4. **Narration goes in `br comments add`** on the round bead as the round
   progresses, matching the loop shape (plan, run, learn, edit).
5. **On close, the round bead is authoritative.** The working markdown file
   is deleted, never committed — a second, uncommitted-but-lingering copy of
   the same round is exactly the failure this feature removes.
6. **The closing step is mandatory**, built into the `qa-review` skill
   itself as a defined step, not a manual call left to whoever is running the
   round. Two rounds in a row already skipped it by default; an optional step
   is not a fix.

## User Stories

1. As the maintainer running a qa-review round, I want the round to close
   into a bead automatically, so that I don't have to remember to decide the
   working file's fate every time.
2. As an agent picking up a bug found during a past round, I want to see
   which round produced it, so that I have the round's full context without
   reconstructing it from a conversation.
3. As an agent or maintainer looking at repo history, I want closed rounds to
   be greppable via `br`/`bv`, so that "what did we test and find in round
   N" doesn't require finding an untracked file that may not exist anymore.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a qa-review round following the (updated) skill's closing step, when
   the round ends, then exactly one `chore`/`qa-round` bead exists with the
   round's plan/results as its description, `--external-ref` set to the
   session id, and the working markdown file is gone (not committed,
   deleted).
2. Given findings filed during a round, when the round closes, then each
   finding bead is a child of that round's bead (`--parent <round-id>`).
3. Given the `qa-review` skill's own instructions, when an agent reads them
   top to bottom, then the closing step reads as mandatory, not optional or
   merely suggested.
4. Given the two rounds currently sitting as untracked files in this repo
   (`QA_REVIEW.md`, `QA_REVIEW-permissions-round.md`), when this feature
   ships, then both have been retroactively closed under the new rule: round
   beads created, their already-filed findings re-parented under the correct
   round bead, and the two files deleted.

## Implementation Notes

- Skill file: `/home/lotso/dotfiles/agentskills/.config/agentskills/qa-review/SKILL.md`
  (and its `TEMPLATE.md`) — add the closing step here.
- `--external-ref` dovetails with the maintainer's existing global commit rule
  (`Refs <id>` for named sessions/issues in commit messages).
- The transcript-export/blog-publishing round's findings are:
  `louiselm-dim` (closed), `louiselm-euj` (open), `louiselm-d2o` (open),
  `louiselm-xrf` (open) — all currently un-parented, all belong under that
  round's bead.
- The permissions round (working file: `QA_REVIEW-permissions-round.md`,
  origin `louiselm-4wx`) reports "all six cases passed" with three

title: Add mandatory closing step to the qa-review skill
description:
## What

Add a mandatory closing step to the `qa-review` skill
(`/home/lotso/dotfiles/agentskills/.config/agentskills/qa-review/SKILL.md`,
alongside `TEMPLATE.md`) that runs at the end of every round:

1. Create one bead: `br create -t chore --labels qa-round --description-file
   <working-file> --external-ref <session-id>`.
2. Re-parent (or newly create, if not yet filed) any findings from the round
   under that bead: `br create -t bug --parent <round-id>` for new findings;
   `br update <finding-id> --parent <round-id>` for findings already filed
   during the round.
3. Append round narration to the round bead via `br comments add` as the
   round progresses (not just at the end).
4. On close: delete the working markdown file. Never commit it.
5. State explicitly that individual test cases are never beaded — only
   findings are.

This step must read as required, not optional — the skill has twice let
rounds end without deciding the working file's fate.

## Why

Parent feature: louiselm-ri1. Full rationale, rejected alternatives, and
acceptance criteria live there — this task is the skill-file change only.

- The `qa-review` skill's closing step is unambiguous on a cold read: an
  agent running a round for the first time reaches it and cannot mistake it
  for optional.
- `TEMPLATE.md` (if it currently ships a working-file template) reflects
  that the file is scratch, not a committed artifact.

title: Report receiver reachability and per-device delivery health
description:
## Goal
Make receiver status distinguish a running process from a phone-reachable and recently used delivery path.

## Scope
- In scope: configured bind and advertised endpoint in status; loopback-only/unconfigured classification; paired-device count; durable last successful delivery per device; warning when paired devices exist without a phone-reachable endpoint; health response semantics needed by the Android endpoint check.
- Out of scope: phone queue contents on the receiver, cloud monitoring, notifications, public availability probing, transcription-health redesign, and installation of network software.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. status reports the configured profile, bind, advertised endpoint, loopback-only state, and paired-device count without exposing credentials, tokens, environments, or capture contents.
2. Successful new and idempotent duplicate uploads durably update the authenticated device last-delivery time only after the capture is present in the canonical store.
3. Device status reports last successful delivery, or clearly reports none, and survives receiver restart.
4. A loopback-only receiver with paired devices reports a degraded actionable warning rather than healthy delivery.
5. The HTTP health response supplies only the bounded identity/reachability evidence required for safe same-receiver endpoint validation.
6. Authentication failures, interrupted uploads, digest conflicts, and storage failures do not advance last-delivery state.

## Testing
- Start with failing Rust pairing, receiver, and CLI status tests.
- Cover successful create, duplicate retry after acknowledgement loss, rejected identity/credential, failed ingest, restart persistence, and sanitized status output.
- Run cargo fmt, clippy under the repository policy, and the complete capture-service test suite.

## Notes
Keep delivery health separate from transcription health. The server cannot know the phone queue depth and must not pretend otherwise.
close_reason: Implemented receiver reachability and durable per-device delivery health

title: Resumed session picker row exposes raw prompt text before ready status
description:
The attached-session picker exposes the resumed session's raw initial prompt before its normal status metadata, making that row visually inconsistent and harder to scan. In the picker, an existing session appears as a compact identity/status/metadata row, while a session resumed from persisted state starts with a long `[AGENTS.md](file:///...)` prompt fragment and only then shows `ready`; the prompt content should not be the primary identity shown in this picker.

## Observed

Screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260823_0543_1920x1200_1787456626.png` (1920x1200, captured 2026-08-23 05:43 local time).

The picker shows two attached sessions. The first row is compact:

`session-1 · ready · skills: native · codex/01a02c74-a9f9-7222-9378-059083ea6f87 · Mode=Agent (full access) · Collaboration mode=Default · Model=GPT-5.6-Luna · Reasoning effort...`

The resumed second row begins with prompt text:

`session-3 · [@AGENTS.md](file:///home/lotso/code/acp-llm-adapter/AGENTS.md)can you takeover this PR, it fails, fix it ready · loaded · skills: native · codex/...`

The relevant picker path is `lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:2117-2121`, where attached sessions use `session_summary(session:inspect())`; `session_identity` at `lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:313-334` concatenates the session name, status, loaded marker, skills policy, and agent/acp id. The screenshot demonstrates that the resumed session's inspected identity/name (or equivalent state field) contains unsanitized prompt content, unlike the normal session row.

## Symptoms

- A resumed session has a radically different row shape from a freshly created session.
- Long prompt content consumes the picker row and can obscure the stable status and session identity.
- The row is misleadingly centered on prompt text even though the user is choosing an attached session, not reviewing prompt history.

## Root cause

Not fully confirmed. The picker formatter is shared and deterministic; it delegates the displayed identity to inspected session state. The likely defect is that resumed-session restoration populates a display identity/name field from the persisted initial prompt, or fails to provide a bounded title, and the picker does not sanitize or bound that field before rendering. Confirm by tracing the loaded-session state construction and comparing it with fresh-session state.

## Why it was not caught

Current picker coverage appears to exercise the formatter/state path without a realistic persisted session whose initial prompt contains a Markdown file link and a long takeover request. No regression fixture captures the visual/row-shape difference between fresh and resumed sessions.

## Fix direction

Keep the picker’s stable identity first: use a bounded, single-line display name/title derived from the persisted session title when available, otherwise the session id or agent/session id. Do not use raw prompt content as the primary picker label. Sanitize and bound any user/session-provided display text at the shared picker formatting boundary, while preserving the full prompt in the session transcript.

## Acceptance

- A regression test covers a resumed/persisted session with a long Markdown/file-link prompt.
- The attached-session picker row remains compact and starts with a stable session name/id and status (for example `session-3 · ready · loaded ...`), with no raw initial prompt preceding those fields.
- Fresh and resumed sessions use the same picker row shape, subject only to their legitimate metadata differences.

## Not covered

This report does not claim that loading or session readiness is functionally broken. It also does not prescribe whether the final label should be a persisted title, session id, or agent/session id; that choice should follow the existing session identity contract.
close_reason: Fixed at lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:2651 by using the stable discovered session_id as the attached session name instead of the ACP-provided title, which may contain the initial prompt. Updated tests/ui/chat_spec.lua with a Markdown/file-link prompt title and asserted the load options use prior-acp. Focused chat suite: 94 passed. Full MiniTest suite: 351 passed. stylua --check . passed. lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning passed. Full suite emitted existing skill-discovery/write warnings but had 0 failures.

title: Switching sessions leaves chat input in Normal mode
description:
Switching between attached LouiseLM chat sessions leaves the selected chat buffer in Normal mode, so typing and pressing Enter does not submit a prompt. The session appears idle and its ACP process remains alive, but no new prompt reaches the agent until the user manually presses i.

## Observed

Seen 2026-08-22 in the same Neovim instance with Codex sessions codex/01a02a74-274c-79d2-967e-597c37d997ed and the current session. The old session transcript stopped at its previous task completion; no new user turn was recorded after switching to it and pressing Enter. The associated ACP processes were alive.

## Symptoms

- Switching sessions succeeds, but the selected chat does not accept a prompt normally.
- Text typed after switching is handled as Normal-mode input; Enter does not submit.
- Manually pressing i restores the expected behavior.

## Root cause

`lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:2027` (`Chat:switch`) changes the current buffer and renders it, but does not restore insert mode or move the cursor to the prompt. `lua/louiselm/ui/picker.lua` stops insert mode before opening the session picker. Initial attachment calls `startinsert` at `lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:1837`, but switching does not.

## Why it was not caught

Existing switch tests assert buffer/session selection and queued prompt behavior, but do not assert the editor mode or cursor state after switching through the picker.

## Fix direction

Make `Chat:switch` restore the selected view prompt cursor and insert mode, using the same narrow behavior as initial attachment. Add a headless regression assertion for switching to a session and submitting through the restored prompt.

## Acceptance

- A regression test fails before the fix and passes after it.
- After `:LouiselmSwitchSession` selects a session, the cursor is on that session prompt and Neovim is in Insert mode.
- Pressing Enter submits a prompt to the selected session without requiring a manual i.

## Not covered

No changes to ACP process lifecycle or persisted Codex sessions are required.
close_reason: Fixed in the working tree: Chat:switch now restores the selected prompt cursor and Insert mode. Regression test tests/ui/chat_spec.lua 'restores prompt input after switching sessions' failed before the fix and passes after it. Verification: focused chat_spec.lua 87/87; full MiniTest suite 334/334; stylua --check . passed; lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning passed; git diff --check passed. The full test output still emits pre-existing skill-discovery/write warnings, but no test failures.

title: Native skill picker never resolves against the real Claude ACP adapter (exact description match rejects its scope-annotation suffix)
description:
Native skill invocation via the picker never resolves against the real Claude Code ACP adapter, because Claude appends a scope annotation to every advertised command description and the correlation code requires exact equality.

## Observed

Found 2026-08-20 during a qa-review round for louiselm-2w4 (native ACP command invocation, commit 763ba78), before any human test case was run -- by inspecting a pre-existing real ACP debug log on this machine (louiselm.nvim itself is run through claude-agent-acp for this very session).

Log: ~/.local/state/acp-llm-adapter/20260820-100019-702281-claude-agent-acp-stdout-jsonrpc.log, line 3 (session/update, sessionUpdate=available_commands_update). The "grill-me" entry:

  "name":"grill-me","description":"Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases. (user)","input":null

The local SKILL.md at ~/.config/agentskills/generated/grill-me/SKILL.md has description:

  Grill the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea. Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.

-- identical text, but the advertised one carries a trailing " (user)" that the local one does not.

Checked systematically: parsed all 76 entries in that available_commands_update payload. Every command whose name matches a configured local skill path (br, bvr, caveman, caveman-commit, caveman-help, caveman-review, grill-me, htmx, karpathy-guidelines, lightweight-charts, playwright-cli, playwright-qa-review, ponytail*, qa-review, rscss, rtk, rust-architecture, terraform-skill, to-beads*, write-a-skill -- 27 total) ends with " (user)". Claude's own built-in/plugin commands in the same payload (compact, config, model, doctor, mcp, loop, schedule, security-review, etc.) do not have this suffix.

## Symptoms

- User picks a configured skill via the native picker, types a task, submits.
- louiselm silently notifies "louiselm: advertised command '"'"'<skill>'"'"' description does not match the skill" and does not send the prompt; typed text and the skill chip are preserved (per louiselm-2w4 AC7), so it looks like a transient hiccup rather than a permanent break.
- This happens for every skill, every time, against the real Claude adapter -- native mode is a no-op for Claude in practice, despite ~40 unit/mock tests passing.

## Root cause

lua/louiselm/skills/native_command.lua, description_matches() (around line 45): compares the whitespace-normalized advertised description to the whitespace-normalized local skill.description (or skill.short_description) with `==`. Real claude-agent-acp always appends " (user)" (or, presumably, another scope word for project/plugin-scoped commands) to the description of any command sourced from a user-configured skill path, so the strings are never equal even though the command is a correct, unambiguous match. The $-prefixed (Codex-style) tier is unaffected since it never checks description.

## Why it was not caught

Every existing test (tests/skills_spec.lua resolve_command cases, tests/ui/chat_spec.lua native-picker cases, tests/mock/agent_spec.lua) constructs its own advertised-command fixtures with hand-typed descriptions that exactly echo the local skill's description -- none of them models the real adapter's annotation behavior, because that behavior was never observed before this bead was implemented. The acceptance criteria for louiselm-2w4 specified "the whitespace-normalized advertised description matches the local SKILL.md description" without anticipating an adapter-appended suffix.

## Fix direction

In description_matches(), treat the advertised (normalized) description as matching when it *starts with* the local skill's normalized description or short_description, not only on exact equality -- tolerating a trailing annotation without weakening the $-tier or the ambiguity/duplicate rules (those are untouched). Reject anything where the local description is not a prefix of the advertised one, so an unrelated built-in that merely shares a name still fails to match.

## Acceptance

- A regression test in tests/skills_spec.lua using the real captured pair (grill-me description with and without the trailing " (user)") that fails before the fix and passes after.
- Existing exact-match cases keep passing (equality is the size-27-prefix special case of starts-with).

## Not covered

- Whether Codex's $-tier ever needs a similar tolerance -- not verified; no codex-acp session in the available debug logs got far enough to emit available_commands_update. Left as a follow-up if codex turns out to need it too.
- Whether Claude ever uses a different annotation word (e.g. "(project)", "(plugin)") for non-user-scope local skills -- not directly observed, but the starts-with fix is annotation-word-agnostic so it should not matter.
close_reason: Fixed in c230f8c. Root cause: description_matches() in lua/louiselm/skills/native_command.lua required exact whitespace-normalized equality; real claude-agent-acp appends a scope annotation (" (user)") to every command sourced from a user-configured skill path. Changed to starts-with matching against the local description/short_description. Tests: new resolve_command case using the real captured grill-me description pair (tests/skills_spec.lua), plus full existing resolve_command suite re-verified green. Gates: full mini.test suite green (287 cases), stylua and lua-language-server clean. No deviation from filed acceptance criteria. Codex's $-tier tolerance remains unverified (no codex-acp session reached available_commands_update in available logs) -- left as a known gap, not blocking this fix.

title: br scheduler --json returns empty labels, hiding label-based routing from the command AGENTS.md prefers
description:
`br scheduler --json` emits `labels: []` for every recommendation, even when the
issue demonstrably carries labels. The field exists in the `br.scheduler.v1`
envelope and is always empty, so it reads as authoritative absence rather than
as missing data.

## Evidence (br 0.3.2, 2026-08-21)

`br scheduler --limit 6 --json`, labels as reported by the scheduler versus the
same issues via `br label list`:

| issue | scheduler | `br label list` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| louiselm-ce6.21 | `[]` | acp, chat, multimodal, qa-finding, ready-for-agent, ui |
| louiselm-ufx | `[]` | ui |
| louiselm-qbr.1.11 | `[]` | android, capture, qa-finding, ready-for-agent, ui |
| louiselm-qbr.1.12 | `[]` | android, capture, pairing, qa-finding, ready-for-agent, ui |
| louiselm-qbr.1.14 | `[]` | android, capture, privacy, qa-finding, ready-for-agent, ui, usability |
| louiselm-qbr.1.15 | `[]` | android, capture, qa-finding, ready-for-agent, status, ui |

`br list --json` and `br show --json` both populate `labels` correctly for the
same issues, so this is specific to the scheduler envelope.

## Why it matters here

AGENTS.md section 2 tells agents to prefer `br scheduler` over hand-scanning,
because it excludes claimed work and explains its ranking. An agent that follows
that instruction receives issues stripped of their labels.

That closes both routes for label-aware work selection at once. `br scheduler`
has no `--label`/`--label-any` filter of its own (unlike `br ready`), so
server-side filtering is unavailable; and because the returned labels are empty,
client-side filtering on the scheduler's own output is unavailable too. Any
convention that routes work by label is invisible to the command the contract
tells agents to use.

This was found while designing capability-based work routing
(`needs-capability:*` labels). It is not blocking that design -- `br ready`
carries labels and supports `-l` and `--label-any` -- but it does mean the
documented preference for `br scheduler` and label-based routing are mutually
exclusive until one of them changes.

## Not this repository

This is a defect in `br` (beads), not in louiselm. Filed here because it
constrains a louiselm workflow decision and would otherwise be lost. Upstream
report still to be raised.

## Suggested resolution

Populate `labels` in the `br.scheduler.v1` issue envelope from the same source
`br list --json` uses. A `--label`/`--label-any` filter matching `br ready`
would be a separate, larger ask.

description:

comments.author: codex/01a02e9a-7870-71b0-a820-c37f696a05d3
comments.text:
Investigation 2026-08-23:
- LouiseLM config runs the Codex Agent with the default skills policy native; therefore LouiseLM does not discover or inject its catalog for this Agent.
- Installed @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp version 1.6.2 refreshes Codex-native skills by forwarding skills/list with forceReload=true. It does not construct or rewrite individual skill locations.
- On disk, generated/.system exists but contains only imagegen, openai-docs, plugin-creator, review-agent, skill-creator, and skill-installer. karpathy-guidelines exists at generated/karpathy-guidelines/SKILL.md, not below .system.
- Therefore the invalid location was produced downstream by the Codex native skill runtime, outside LouiseLM's catalog/discovery code.

No LouiseLM code change is safe: native mode intentionally delegates discovery to the Agent. A local workaround is to set agents.codex.skills.policy = "inject", which makes LouiseLM emit its independently discovered, correct paths, but changes Codex from native skill handling to injected catalog handling and requires maintainer approval.

The proposed upstream fix is to preserve the actual discovered path and validate it exists. codex-acp's open issue list has no matching path-location report; this belongs to openai/codex.
